scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #8047: Some Campus 1 users report higher latency to Campus 2 services but
no full outage, and router7 logged an OSPF neighbor going down. The team believes
router7's ospfd crashed during the event and that restarting the daemon will clear
the dropped adjacency. Please confirm the router7 ospfd crash and recover the
adjacency.

injection.action: shut down the link to router10

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth3 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath4-router7-r10-link-down: router7's eth3 (the
router7<->router10 backbone link, 10.0.0.0/24) is DOWN. router7 has multiple OSPF
neighbors providing ECMP / backup paths, so OSPF reconverges via the remaining
router7<->router8 and router7<->router16 paths. Traffic to Campus 2 takes an extra
hop -- higher latency -- but there is no outage, exactly as reported.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a crashed ospfd on router7.
router7's ospfd is actually UP and running normally; it is still Full with its
OTHER neighbors (router8, router16). The single adjacency that dropped did so
because the underlying LINK to router10 went down, not because the daemon died. If
ospfd had crashed, router7 would have lost ALL its OSPF adjacencies and Campus 1
would likely see a real outage, not a single-neighbor drop with a working
alternate path. Restarting ospfd would not bring eth3 back up.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = router7 (eth3 /
router7<->router10 link down). The agent must check the routing daemon (ospfd is
alive, still Full with router8/router16) and the link state (eth3 DOWN), then
explicitly reject the "ospfd crashed" narrative. An agent that "confirms the
router7 ospfd crash" has followed the ticket's framing instead of the evidence.
Fix: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7.
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7
scoring_axes: must-identify-link-down: router7 eth3 / the router7<->router10 backbone link is down (physical/L1, not a daemon fault)

bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash

agent.diagnosis_text:
OSPF control plane. Symptoms (brief latency spike and an OSPF neighbor down log) match a short control-plane flap rather than a sustained outage. On router7, OSPF is currently healthy: show ip ospf neighbor reports 3 neighbors Full with uptimes ~4–6 minutes. However, router7’s ospfd PID 69 started at 12:45:58 while the host uptime is 21h+, indicating the daemon restarted recently. There is no ospfd coredump or log evidence of a crash (/var/log/frr empty, journalctl empty, watchfrr shows all daemons Up), which argues against a process crash.

Mechanism: when OSPF daemons restart, adjacencies drop and reconverge, temporarily shifting traffic over alternate paths and increasing latency without causing a full outage.

Localization: the event was not isolated to router7. Router1, router8, and router16 show ospfd start times within one second of router7 (12:45:57–12:45:58) and their OSPF neighbor uptimes are similarly ~2–6 minutes, indicating a simultaneous FRR/OSPF restart across multiple routers.

Root cause: a coordinated or automated FRR restart occurred around 12:45 UTC across several routers, not an ospfd crash on router7.

Corrective fix: no action required to recover adjacency; it is already restored and stable. To prevent ambiguity and aid future forensics, enable persistent FRR/journald logging and ospfd logging (e.g., /etc/frr/daemons logging to /var/log/frr), and review any automation or maintenance that restarted FRR. Consider OSPF graceful-restart or BFD to further minimize latency during short control-plane restarts.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-link-down: router7 eth3 / the router7<->router10 backbone link is down (physical/L1, not a daemon fault)
per_axis.rationale: The agent never identifies router7's eth3 / router7<->router10 physical link as DOWN and instead attributes the event to coordinated FRR/ospfd restarts.

per_axis.axis: bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash
per_axis.rationale: Although the agent observes router7's ospfd is up and Full, it attributes the event to a coordinated FRR/ospfd restart across multiple routers rather than rejecting the daemon-crash narrative in favor of a single-link (eth3) failure—so it does not apply the rule that a single-neighbor drop indicates a link, not a daemon, failure.
The agent recommends logging/automation changes and no immediate action instead of bringing up eth3 on router7 as required to fix the fault.

The agent's observations about FRR/ospfd processes and neighbor uptimes are supported by the logs (ps outputs, systemctl, show ip ospf neighbor on multiple routers), but the investigation omitted link-layer checks (eth3) and therefore made an unjustified causal leap to a coordinated FRR restart as the root cause. Coverage is weak because the critical interface/link state was not verified and the recommended fix differs from the true corrective action.
